title: About
text: Hello! My name is Juan Toro Fabra and this is my personal blog. I’m a physics student at EPFL, originally from Madrid, Spain. I will be using this blog to share some ideas I come across, mainly related to physics/math but also hopefully some other things as well.

title: Ferromagnetic properties of the game of Go
text: Lately I’ve been playing some Go with my friend Juan. Go is a Chinese board game where you basically have to place stones on a grid to capture territory. A group of stones is captured when it loses all its liberties (the empty points adjacent to it) i.e. when it is completely surrounded by enemy stones. As the nerds we are, we quickly noticed some similarities between the game of Go and the Ising model for ferromagnetism.

title: Ferromagnetic properties of the game of Go
text: Lately I’ve been playing some Go with my friend Juan. Go is a Chinese board game where you basically have to place stones on a grid to capture territory. A group of stones is captured when it loses all its liberties (the empty points adjacent to it) i.e. when it is completely surrounded by enemy stones. As the nerds we are, we quickly noticed some similarities between the game of Go and the Ising model for ferromagnetism.

title: Ferromagnetic properties of the game of Go
text:
What is the Ising model
The Ising model is a model for ferromagnetism developed in the 1920s. Essentially, it treats a material as a grid of tiny magnets (spins) that can point either up or down. The probability of finding the material in a given configuration (some combination of up and down spins) depends on its energy, which depends on two things (more in Annex A): 1. the external magnetic field, which pushes every spin in its direction, and 2. the interaction between neighbouring spins. When neighbours prefer to point the same way, the spins can align on their own, even without an external field, and the material is ferromagnetic.
The similarities lie in the fact that liberties in Go are like the external field in the Ising model (your orthogonal neighbours affect whether you stay alive or not), territory can be white/black like spins are up/down, and that you end up with blocks of territory (lonely pieces die).



Left: spins on a grid, coupled to their neighbours by \(J\) and pushed by the external field \(h\). Right: the textbook Ising model without external field. Hot (disordered) and cold (the spins align on their own).

title: Ferromagnetic properties of the game of Go
text:
The model
I now set out to try to describe predicting the outcome of Go games with this model, and hopefully try to see if it makes sense to define some notion of ferromagnetism for the game.
Grosso modo this is the solution I came up with: start from a given position, and treat the existing stones as an external magnetic field. Then, with that external field, sample the probability distribution of an Ising model and take the prediction of the final outcome as the expected spins.

Essentially what we want is to find the parameters that assign low energies to the real final territory given some position and high energies to the rest.
This model has three main things to be learned: how the color of a stone affects the external magnetic field around it (\(w\)), how the position in the board affects the external magnetic field (\(b\)), and finally the coupling between neighbours (\(J\)). How many parameters? \(w\) is a 5x5 kernel, \(b\) is a 9x9 map (the entire board), and \(J\) is a 3x3 kernel. However from symmetry we can reduce this to 6 parameters for \(w\), 15 parameters for \(b\), and 2 for \(J\). Total 23. The next step is to find a dataset to train these parameters, and based on the shape of \(J\) we will be able to see if Go can be described through ferromagnetic coupling.
To build the training set I downloaded the KataGo model and made it play about 7000 games against itself, from which I extracted a position in the middle of the game and the final territory assigned once the game was done. Then I trained the parameters with PyTorch to maximize the log likelihood of the final territory in all the games given the model parameters (see Annex B).
Once we have the trained parameters we can compare what the model predicts will be the outcome (see Annex C) given a starting position and compare it to the actual outcome.



Three games from the test set. Blue is black’s territory, orange is white’s.


This doesn’t seem too bad, but let’s take a look at the parameters. The first thing is that the baseline with no spin coupling already does fairly well, so it’s not immediately clear whether or not coupling is really needed.
From the coupling parameters we also see that only orthogonal neighbours couple, which makes sense given the rules of the game (although more than I expected).
In numbers, both models get about 80 % of the points right, so the coupling doesn’t help to guess each point. Where it does help is with the whole board at once: the log-loss of the real final territory is cut in half, because the model knows that territory comes in blocks.
And \(J = 0.77\) is a strong coupling, the textbook 2D Ising model (infinite board, no external field) orders into a magnet above \(J \approx 0.44\). Our board is small and the stones act as a field so this is only a rough reference, but it is something.

The coupling also changes how the stones create a field. Without coupling the kernel \(w\) is a broad blob with large weights even far from the center. Every square is guessed on its own, so a stone has to spread its colour over its whole area of influence by itself. With coupling the kernel is very local and even has a negative weight on its four orthogonal neighbours.
The bias \(b\) is and small noisy but we can recognise some areas and positions that vaguely make sense knowing the game. Again a big change between coupling and non-coupling cases.



The bias \(b\) on each square from the player to move’s point of view.


Also, the average predictions with and without coupling look very similar, but that’s only the average. If instead we sample two possible endings from each model for the same game they change a lot.
Without coupling every point is drawn on its own while with coupling you get blobs of the same color like in a real game.



Two endings sampled from each model for the first game above.

title: Ferromagnetic properties of the game of Go
text:
Ferromagnetism?
Of course Go is not Ising. A group lives or dies all at once, a stone that will be captured pushes the wrong way, shape matters and not just the number of stones, our domain is really small, etc etc… Our analogy ends here.
But we can forget about these silly limitations and imagine a hypothetical where the game of Go was just our fitted Ising model. Would it be ferromagnetic?
Let’s see two ways to find a ferromagnet.

Heat it up and at some critical temperature \(T_c\) it loses its magnetization, with a peak in the susceptibility (how much the magnetization \(M = \sum_i s_i\) responds to small changes).
Below \(T_c\) if you add an external field and then remove it, it stays magnetized (hysteresis). Our model has no temperature, but we can give it one by dividing the energy by \(T\) so that \(T = 1\) is the trained model (details in Annex D).

Let’s start without stones on an empty board (no external field).

There is a clear peak at \(T_c \approx 1.5\), and our model (\(T = 1\)) sits below it, so with no external field it is already magnetized.

And it has memory. After a push and back to zero field it stays 96 % magnetized, while above \(T_c\) (\(T = 2.5\)) it just follows the field and forgets it. So the coupling the model learned from Go is, on its own, the coupling of a magnet.
Again this is not surprising knowing the coupling kernel from the training, but it still learnt that all on its own from looking at games. It could have also learnt a different coupling or no coupling at all.

title: Ferromagnetic properties of the game of Go
text:
The answer
Yes, but not exactly.
To end the post here’s a whole game move by move with its corresponding prediction at each point.
Notice how with few stones (small external field) the whole board leans towards one color like in the empty board case. It starts to get good around the middle (trained on mid-games). Also, towards the end it doesn’t realize the white pieces A4-A5-A6 were dead from the start. Still, it looks nice.



A test game move by move, with the prediction of the Ising model at each move. At the end, the real final territory.

title: Ferromagnetic properties of the game of Go
text:
Annex

A. The model
Each point \(i\) of the board has a spin \(s_i = \pm 1\), its final owner, seen from the player to move (\(+1\) for the player to move, \(-1\) for the opponent). Neutral points are left out. The position is \(X_k \in \{+1, -1, 0\}\) (own stone, opponent stone, empty). The model is
\[
P(s \mid X) = \frac{1}{Z(X)} \exp\Big( \sum_i h_i s_i + \sum_{\langle ij \rangle} J_{ij} s_i s_j \Big),
\qquad
h_i = \sum_{\mathbf r} w(\mathbf r)\, X_{i + \mathbf r} + b_i ,
\]
where \(Z(X)\) is the partition function, a sum over \(2^{81}\) configurations. The temperature is absorbed in the parameters (\(T = 1\)). The field \(h\) is a convolution of the stones with a \(5\times5\) kernel \(w\) plus a bias \(b_i\) per square. \(J_{ij}\) is \(J_\text{orto}\) for orthogonal neighbours, \(J_\text{diag}\) for diagonal ones and \(0\) otherwise.
All parameters are invariant under the 8 symmetries of the board. That leaves 6 values for \(w\), 15 for \(b\) and 2 for \(J\), 23 in total.
If all spins but one are fixed,
\[
P(s_i \mid s_{\setminus i}, X) = \sigma(2 s_i H_i),
\qquad H_i = h_i + \sum_j J_{ij} s_j ,
\qquad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} .
\]
\(H_i\) is the local field, the field of the stones plus that of the neighbours. Sampling uses this formula.


B. Training
The negative log-likelihood per point is minimized over the 5535 training games,
\[
\mathcal L = -\frac{1}{N_\text{points}} \sum_{n} \log P(s^{(n)} \mid X^{(n)}) = \frac{1}{N_\text{points}} \sum_n \Big[ \log Z(X^{(n)}) - \log Z_\text{fixed}(X^{(n)}) \Big],
\]
where \(Z_\text{fixed}\) is the same sum restricted to the configurations that agree with the real owners. The exponent is linear in \((w, b, J)\), so \(\mathcal L\) is convex.
\(Z\) is computed column by column. A column \(\sigma \in \{\pm 1\}^9\) has 512 states, and \(J\) only couples neighbouring columns, so
\[
Z(X) = \sum_{\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_9} \prod_{k=1}^{9} e^{\phi_k(\sigma_k)} \prod_{k=1}^{8} e^{\psi(\sigma_k, \sigma_{k+1})},
\]
\[
\phi_k(\sigma) = \sum_f h_{f,k}\, \sigma_f + J_\text{orto} \sum_f \sigma_f \sigma_{f+1},
\qquad
\psi(\sigma, \sigma') = J_\text{orto} \sum_f \sigma_f \sigma'_f + J_\text{diag} \sum_f \big( \sigma_f \sigma'_{f+1} + \sigma_{f+1} \sigma'_f \big).
\]
This is a transfer matrix: a vector of 512 entries multiplied 9 times by the \(512 \times 512\) matrix \(e^{\psi}\) and the diagonal factors \(e^{\phi_k}\). The product is done in log space to avoid overflow. The gradient comes from PyTorch, and LBFGS converges in a few minutes. \(Z\) was checked against the brute-force sum on \(3\times3\) and \(3\times4\) boards. On \(13\times13\) there would be 8192 states per column, so this only works for small boards.


C. Prediction
The prediction is the magnetization of each point, \(m_i = \langle s_i \rangle\), and \(P(\text{player to move owns } i) = (1 + m_i)/2\). It is computed exactly as \(m_i = \partial \log Z / \partial h_i\), differentiating the transfer matrix computation with PyTorch.
The sampled endings use Gibbs sampling: each spin is redrawn with \(P(s_i = +1 \mid \text{rest}) = \sigma(2H_i)\), 1000 sweeps from a random board. Without coupling each point is drawn independently with probability \((1 + m_i)/2\).


D. Temperature and hysteresis
A temperature is added to the trained model,
\[
P_T(s \mid X) = \frac{1}{Z_T} \exp\Big[ \frac{1}{T} \Big( \sum_i h_i s_i + \sum_{\langle ij \rangle} J_{ij} s_i s_j \Big) \Big],
\]
so \(T = 1\) is the trained model. With \(M = \sum_i s_i\) and a uniform field \(H\) on every point, the susceptibility is
\[
\frac{\partial \langle M \rangle}{\partial H} = \frac{1}{T} \big( \langle M^2 \rangle - \langle M \rangle^2 \big).
\]
On a finite board without field \(\langle M \rangle = 0\) by symmetry, so \(|M|\) is used instead, per point (\(N = 81\)):
\[
m = \frac{\langle |M| \rangle}{N}, \qquad \chi = \frac{\langle M^2 \rangle - \langle |M| \rangle^2}{N\, T}.
\]
On the empty board, Gibbs sampling was run for 31 temperatures between 0.25 and 4, with 256 chains, 300 sweeps of burn-in and 1000 of measurement.
For the hysteresis, at fixed \(T\), \(H\) goes from \(-4\) to \(+4\) in steps of 0.2 and back, without restarting the chains, with 100 sweeps per step. The remanence is \(m\) at \(H = 0\) on the way down.

title: Everybody lives in Ecuador
text:
Artistic rendition of a high-dimensional watermelon
Pick a point uniformly at random in the unit ball of \(\mathbb R^n\). For high enough \(n\) this point will practically always fall along the surface, i.e. high-dimensional watermelons have no red part. But not only that, this is also true for the equators of high-dimensional spheres. Let’s see why.

title: Everybody lives in Ecuador
text:
Warm-up: the surface
First: a random point in the unit ball is practically always near its surface. Since we choose the point uniformly at random, the chance of being near the surface is the same as the volume of a thin shell of width \(\varepsilon\) near the surface. Like an onion.
Shrinking the unit ball by a factor \(1-\varepsilon\) gives exactly \(\{\|x\| \le 1-\varepsilon\}\), and shrinking multiplies volumes by \(1-\varepsilon\) once per coordinate, so
\[
\mathbb P(\|x\| \le 1-\varepsilon) = (1-\varepsilon)^n \longrightarrow 0.
\]
For \(\varepsilon = 0.01\) and \(n=3\) the inner part holds \(97\%\) of the volume, for \(n=100\) it holds \(37\%\) and for \(n=1000\) it holds \(0.004\%\). The rest lies in the thin shell \(1-\varepsilon < \|x\| \le 1\) near the surface.
If we sample points, their distance to the center has density \(n r^{n-1}\) (the derivative of \(r^n\)), and as \(n\) grows it gets closer and closer to \(r = 1\).





Distance to the center of uniform points in the ball. Black curves are the exact density n r^(n-1). Log vertical axis.

title: Everybody lives in Ecuador
text:
Setup for the equator
Now let’s define what equator means. For a given unit vector \(e_1\), the equator is the hyperplane \(\{x_1 = 0\}\), and the latitude of a point is its coordinate \(x_1\). Being close to the equator means having \(|x_1| < \delta\) for some \(\delta > 0\).
In \(\mathbb R^3\) the equator of a sphere (\(S^2\)) is a circle (\(S^1\)), which feels like a very small part. But in \(\mathbb R^n\) the equator of \(S^{n-1}\) is an \(S^{n-2}\). It only loses one dimension out of \(n\), and in \(\mathbb R^{100000000}\) losing one dimension out of a hundred million may not matter as much.

title: Everybody lives in Ecuador
text:
Slices and slabs
Where does the random point’s latitude \(x_1\) tend to land? It falls between \(t\) and \(t+dt\) with probability proportional to the volume of the thin slab \(\{t < x_1 < t+dt\}\) of the ball. The slab is approximately an \((n-1)\)-dimensional ball of radius \(\sqrt{1-t^2}\) with thickness \(dt\), so its volume is proportional to \(\big(\sqrt{1-t^2}\big)^{n-1}dt =
(1-t^2)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\,dt\). Hence the latitude has density
\[
f_n(t) = c_n\,(1-t^2)^{\frac{n-1}{2}},
\]
where \(c_n\) is some function of \(n\) (we don’t care). We will use it shortly. Also, be careful, the diagram is in 3D but the calculation is for an arbitrary number of dimensions \(n\).









Now let’s find the variance of the latitude \(x_1\). Since \(\mathbb E[x_1]=0\) by symmetry, the variance is \(\mathbb E[x_1^2]\). We also have that \(n\mathbb E[x^2_1]=\mathbb E[\sum^n_i x_i^2] = \int_0^1 r^2\, n r^{n-1}\,dr = n \int_0^1 r^{n+1}\,dr = \frac{n}{n+2}\) so Var\((x_1) = \frac{1}{n+2}\).
For large \(n\) we then have \(x_1 \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\), so \(t^2\) is small and \(f_n(t) = (1-t^2)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}=\exp\!\big(\tfrac{n-1}{2}\ln(1-t^2)\big)\approx e^{-(n-1)t^2/2}\), which is a Gaussian. Hence
\[
x_1 \approx \mathcal N\!\left(0, \tfrac1n\right).
\]
Here is the latitude of sampled points: for \(n=3\) it follows \(f_n\) but is far from Gaussian, while for \(n=20\) and \(n=200\) it is indistinguishable from \(\mathcal N(0,1/(n))\) and narrower each time.





Latitude of uniform points in the ball, against the exact density f_n and the normal approximation.




To see what this means, take the slab \(|x_1| < 0.01\), just 1% of the diameter. Let’s see what percentage of the volume is inside this slab for different dimensions \(n\):

So as \(n\) grows, a thin slab around the equator holds almost all of the volume, and by symmetry this does not depend on which equator we choose.

title: Everybody lives in Ecuador
section: Close to every equator at once?
text:
Close to every equator at once?
But now we run into an issue: if most of the mass is in the slab around one equator, how can it also sit in the slab around a different one?? In reality it isn’t a problem, because the slabs overlap.
Take two different equators and the slabs around them. They both miss the same fraction of the total volume of the ball, let’s call it \(p\). The probability of being in both slabs is at least \(1-2p\), which is still very close to 1 because we already know \(p\) is very small.
This is just the union bound: a point outside the intersection of the slabs \(S_1, \dots, S_k\) must be outside at least one of them, so
\[
\mathbb P\Big(x \notin \bigcap_{j=1}^k S_j\Big) \le \sum_{j=1}^k \mathbb P(x \notin S_j) = kp
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb P\Big(x \in \bigcap_{j=1}^k S_j\Big) \ge 1-kp .
\]
Since \(p\) shrinks exponentially as \(n\) grows, for large enough \(n\) the bound \(1-kp\) stays close to 1 even for many equators and a random point is near all of them at once.
For example, in \(n = 10\,000\) dimensions 99.5% of the points lie within 0.05 of all ten thousand coordinate equators at once, i.e. they have no coordinate larger than \(0.05\). Practically all of them, while their mean distance to the center is \(n/(n+1) \approx 0.9999\).
Of course we still need a finite number of equators and a high enough dimension \(n\), but the point is that the equator slabs are far from disjoint. In 3D two equators of the sphere only meet at two antipodal points, but in \(n\) dimensions the intersection of \(k\) equators is a whole sphere \(S^{n-1-k}\), still huge when \(k \ll n\).

title: Everybody lives in Ecuador
text:
The shadow
To illustrate this, take each sampled point and keep only its first two coordinates \((x_1, x_2)\) i.e. project it on a planem like the shadow of a ball on the floor. Below, each dot is the shadow of one point, and its color is that point’s true distance to the center, \(\|x\|\), computed with all \(n\) coordinates: yellow means the point is on the surface, purple means it is near the center.





Shadows of uniform points of the ball on the (x1, x2) plane. Color is each point’s true distance to the center, |x|.




For \(n=3\) the shadow fills the disk and the colors are mixed: a dot in the middle of the disk may come from the center of the ball or from one of its poles. At \(n=300\) every dot is yellow, so every point sits close to the surface, and yet the shadows form a tiny cloud in the middle. The distance to the center comes from the other \(298\) coordinates, which the shadow cannot see. Since \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are both small, every point is close to the equators \(\{x_1=0\}\) and \(\{x_2=0\}\) at the same time.

title: Everybody lives in Ecuador
text:
Everyone is on everyone’s equator
Every point has its own pole, the direction \(\frac{x}{\|x\|}\). So we can use one random direction \(\theta\) as the pole and ask what latitude another independent random direction \(\theta'\) has. Rotating \(\theta\) to \(e_1\), that latitude is just \(\theta'_1\), and slicing the sphere (the slice at latitude \(t\) is a sphere of radius \(\sqrt{1-t^2}\), tilted) gives it density \(\propto (1-t^2)^{\frac{n-3}{2}}\). With \(t = \cos\varphi\), the angle between the two directions has density
\[
p_n(\varphi) \propto \sin^{n-2}\varphi, \qquad \varphi\in[0,\pi].
\]
For \(n=3\) this is \(\sin\varphi\), fairly spread out. For large \(n\) it becomes a peak at \(90°\) of width \(\sim 1/\sqrt n\) radians: two random directions in \(\mathbb R^{1000}\) are within \(90° \pm 5.4°\) (“basically” orthogonal) of each other with probability about \(99.7\%\).





Angle between two random directions. Black curves are the exact density, proportional to sin^(n-2). Log vertical axis.




The same happens for many directions at once. Below we take \(40\) random directions and color the cosine of the angle between every pair. The diagonal is each direction with itself, so it is always \(1\). For \(n=3\) the rest is a mess of positive and negative values, since 40 directions in 3D cannot all be perpendicular. For \(n=1000\) everything outside the diagonal is close to \(0\): all 40 directions are nearly perpendicular to each other at the same time.





Cosine of the angle between every pair of 40 random directions. White means perpendicular.

title: Everybody lives in Ecuador
text:
Not that crazy
In reality this is all not that counterintuitive. The constraint \(x_1^2+\dots+x_n^2 \le 1\) is shared by \(n\) coordinates, and we saw in the warm-up that for most points it adds up to almost exactly one. One coordinate could take all of it, like \((1,0,\dots,0)\), but almost all of the volume comes from points that spread it evenly \(\sim \frac{1}{n}\). So every coordinate is of order \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\), the point is near every equator while the total still adds up to a radius close to 1.
Even a point like \((1,0,\dots,0)\) is only special in our choice of axes, we could rotate it and it would become a point like the rest with its coordinates spread out.
